questions.stem: In the introductory valence-bond model, name the hybrid-orbital set used for four equivalent electron-domain directions around a central atom, and state how many hybrid orbitals it contains.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: Direct recall/classification with one common notation trap: sp3 denotes a four-orbital hybrid set, not three hybrid orbitals.

qrt.X: the hybrid-orbital set and set size associated with four equivalent electron-domain directions
qrt.Y: the learner can already recognise four bond directions/electron pairs in a supplied simple Lewis structure
qrt.Z: use the defining mapping between four equivalent directions and the introductory hybrid set
qrt.W: state sp3 and four hybrid orbitals
qrt.wrong_idea: Reading the superscript in sp3 as meaning that there are only three hybrid orbitals.
qrt.replacement_rule: The superscript counts p orbitals mixed with one s orbital; 1 + 3 atomic orbitals form four sp3 hybrid orbitals.

answer.summary: In the introductory valence-bond model the set is sp3. Mixing one s and three p atomic orbitals gives four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals, directed tetrahedrally.
reasoning: Identify that four equivalent electron-domain directions require four equivalent directional hybrids in the introductory model.
One s orbital plus three p orbitals are combined, producing four hybrid orbitals.
The conventional label for that set is sp3.

questions.stem: The Lewis structure H2C=O has a double bond from carbon to oxygen and one single bond from carbon to each hydrogen. Explain why the C=O double bond counts as one electron domain around carbon.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: Requires connecting Lewis bond order to a spatial electron-density region and resisting the two-lines-equals-two-domains trap.

qrt.X: why the two bond lines in C=O do not create two independent electron-domain directions around carbon
qrt.Y: the learner already recognises that the double bond connects the same carbon and oxygen atoms
qrt.Z: distinguish bond order/components from the number of spatial electron-density regions around the central atom
qrt.W: explain that C=O occupies one overall C–O direction and therefore contributes one domain
qrt.wrong_idea: Counting the two lines in a double bond as two separate electron domains.
qrt.replacement_rule: Count distinct regions/directions around the chosen central atom; a multiple bond to one neighbour is one region.

answer.summary: The C=O double bond is one electron domain around carbon because both bonding components connect carbon to the same oxygen in the same overall C–O direction. Electron-domain counting treats a single, double or triple bond to one neighbouring atom as one region of electron density.
reasoning: Around carbon, identify the neighbouring atoms/directions: H, H and O.
The double bond has sigma and pi bonding components, but they belong to the same C–O connection rather than two independent directions from carbon.
Therefore the C=O bond contributes one domain, giving three electron domains around carbon in H2C=O.

questions.stem: For CH4, use the known rule for four bonding domains and no central lone pair to assign the carbon hybridisation and electron-domain geometry. Show the domain count.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: A direct application of the four-domain rule once the four C–H bonding domains are counted.

qrt.X: the four C–H bonding domains and absence of a central lone pair
qrt.Y: the four-domain mapping: four electron domains correspond to tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and an sp3 introductory hybrid set
qrt.Z: count the domains, verify the rule applies, then map the count to the model
qrt.W: assign sp3 and tetrahedral geometry after showing a count of four
qrt.wrong_idea: Reading the flat Lewis layout as a square-planar or cross-shaped molecular geometry.
qrt.replacement_rule: Lewis placement is bookkeeping; VSEPR/domain geometry comes from the number of electron-density regions around the central atom.

answer.summary: CH4 has 4 bonding domains + 0 central lone-pair domains = 4 electron domains. In the introductory model carbon is sp3 hybridised, and the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral (ideal angle about 109.5°).
reasoning: Each C–H single bond is one electron domain around carbon, so there are four bonding domains.
There is no lone pair on the central carbon, so the total remains four.
Apply the introductory four-domain mapping: sp3 hybridisation and tetrahedral electron-domain geometry.

questions.stem: NH3 has three N–H single bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen. Translate that information into a labelled diagram showing all four electron domains; distinguish the lone pair from the three bond directions. Do not treat the planar Lewis sketch as the molecular shape.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: The learner must preserve three bonds plus one lone-pair domain while translating a flat Lewis sketch into a non-planar tetrahedral electron-domain arrangement.

qrt.X: the invariant three N–H bonding domains plus one nitrogen lone-pair domain while moving from 2D Lewis notation to a 3D domain picture
qrt.Y: the learner already distinguishes shared pairs from a lone pair in a supplied Lewis structure
qrt.Z: construct four tetrahedral domain directions and map the three bonds and the lone pair onto them
qrt.W: place the lone-pair domain as the fourth tetrahedral direction and distinguish electron-domain geometry from atom-only molecular geometry
qrt.wrong_idea: Copying the planar Lewis sketch as the molecular shape, or putting all four domains in one plane.
qrt.replacement_rule: Preserve the four-domain count first, then map those domains to tetrahedral directions; molecular geometry names atom positions and therefore omits the lone-pair direction.

answer.summary: NH3 has four electron domains around N: three N–H bonding domains and one lone-pair domain. Arrange those four domains tetrahedrally. In a labelled sketch, place N at the centre, show three N–H directions and label the fourth tetrahedral direction as the lone pair. The atom-only molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal; the planar Lewis layout is not the molecular shape.
reasoning: Translate the Lewis information without changing it: three N–H bonds and one nitrogen lone pair.
Four electron domains use four tetrahedral directions in VSEPR.
Only three of those directions end at H atoms; the fourth is the lone-pair domain, so the molecular geometry described by atom positions is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.stem: A model is needed only to describe the overall three-dimensional arrangement of electron domains in NH3; it need not describe the detailed orbital overlap. Choose between VSEPR and a hybrid-orbital overlap diagram, and identify what your chosen model predicts and what it leaves unresolved.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: Requires selecting a model from the stated explanatory job and articulating model boundaries rather than choosing by a familiar hybridisation keyword.

qrt.X: which requested feature—overall electron-domain arrangement or detailed orbital overlap—determines the appropriate model
qrt.Y: VSEPR uses electron-density regions to predict arrangement; hybrid-orbital overlap diagrams address directional orbitals and bonding overlap
qrt.Z: compare each model's explanatory job with the stated target and choose the one whose scope fits
qrt.W: choose VSEPR and state both what it predicts and what orbital-level detail it leaves unresolved
qrt.wrong_idea: Selecting a hybrid-orbital overlap diagram merely because the topic contains the word hybridisation.
qrt.replacement_rule: Choose a model by the question it is being asked to answer and the model's scope, not by a keyword in the chapter title.

answer.summary: Choose VSEPR for the requested job. It predicts how the four electron domains around N arrange in three dimensions: a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry; with three bonding domains and one lone pair, the atom positions give a trigonal-pyramidal NH3 molecular geometry. VSEPR does not specify the detailed atomic-orbital composition, wavefunctions or overlap pattern of each N–H bond; those are questions for an orbital/valence-bond description.
reasoning: Read the target carefully: only the overall three-dimensional arrangement of electron domains is requested.
VSEPR is explicitly a model for arranging electron-density regions around a central atom and therefore matches that target.
State the boundary: VSEPR gives the domain/shape prediction but not detailed orbital construction or overlap, so an orbital-overlap diagram would answer a different, more microscopic question.

questions.stem: For a qualitative orbital sketch, overlap A is end-on along the internuclear axis and overlap B is side-on on opposite sides of that axis. Classify each as sigma or pi overlap and identify the defining feature you used.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: Direct classification from the defining overlap orientation, with a small representation-reading demand.

qrt.X: whether the overlap is oriented along the internuclear axis or side-on across it
qrt.Y: the learner can identify the line joining two nuclei as the internuclear axis
qrt.Z: classify each sketch using the orientation criterion
qrt.W: state A = sigma and B = pi with the defining feature
qrt.wrong_idea: Classifying pi only by seeing a double bond, rather than by the side-on overlap geometry.
qrt.replacement_rule: Sigma and pi classify orbital overlap by symmetry/orientation relative to the internuclear axis; bond multiplicity is a related but different cue.

answer.summary: Overlap A is sigma (σ) overlap because it is end-on along the internuclear axis. Overlap B is pi (π) overlap because it is side-on, with overlap density on opposite sides of the internuclear axis and a nodal plane containing that axis.
reasoning: Use the internuclear axis as the reference line.
End-on/axial overlap is the defining geometry of a sigma bond.
Side-by-side overlap of parallel orbitals on the two sides of the axis is the defining geometry of a pi bond.

questions.stem: For CH4, sketch a three-dimensional arrangement of the four C–H bond directions using a wedge/dash convention or another clearly defined convention. Explain how your drawing differs from a flat cross-shaped Lewis sketch.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: Requires translating four equivalent C–H directions into depth-coded wedge/dash notation and contrasting that with a non-geometric flat Lewis cross.

qrt.X: the four equivalent C–H bond directions that must remain four and become genuinely three-dimensional
qrt.Y: the learner already recognises the four C–H bonds in a Lewis structure
qrt.Z: use the wedge/dash convention to encode in-plane, toward-viewer and away-from-viewer directions
qrt.W: construct a tetrahedral wedge/dash arrangement and explain why it is not a flat cross
qrt.wrong_idea: Treating wedge/dash marks as decorative while retaining a planar 90° cross interpretation.
qrt.replacement_rule: Wedge/dash is depth encoding; the target arrangement is non-coplanar tetrahedral, with ideal angles near 109.5°.

answer.summary: A valid wedge/dash sketch places C at the centre with four C–H directions tetrahedrally: for example, two bonds drawn in the plane, one solid wedge toward the viewer and one hashed wedge behind the plane. The four directions are not coplanar and correspond to ideal tetrahedral angles of about 109.5°, unlike a flat cross-shaped Lewis drawing that is only a 2D connectivity sketch.
reasoning: Keep the invariant: methane has four equivalent C–H bond directions around carbon.
Use wedge/dash notation to encode depth: ordinary line in the page, solid wedge toward the viewer, hashed wedge away.
The resulting tetrahedral set is non-coplanar; a cross-shaped Lewis diagram does not assert four 90° coplanar bond directions.

questions.stem: A nitrogen atom in NF3 has three N–F single bonds and one lone pair. Each fluorine also has lone pairs. Count the electron domains around nitrogen and state which lone pairs belong in that central-atom count.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: Requires applying the domain-count procedure with the local central-atom scope and rejecting visually salient fluorine lone pairs.

qrt.X: which electron pairs belong to the nitrogen-centred domain count
qrt.Y: the learner can identify which atom owns each lone pair in a Lewis structure
qrt.Z: restrict the count to bond regions incident on N plus lone pairs located on N
qrt.W: give four domains around N and exclude all F lone pairs from that central count
qrt.wrong_idea: Counting every lone pair visible anywhere in NF3 when the question asks for domains around nitrogen.
qrt.replacement_rule: Electron-domain counting is local to the chosen central atom: include its bonds and its lone pairs, not lone pairs centred on neighbouring atoms.

answer.summary: Around nitrogen in NF3 there are four electron domains: three N–F bonding domains plus one lone-pair domain on nitrogen. Lone pairs on fluorine belong to fluorine-centred electron domains and are not included in the electron-domain count around nitrogen.
reasoning: Choose the central atom whose domains are being counted: nitrogen.
Count the three N–F bonds as three nitrogen-centred bonding regions and add nitrogen's own lone pair.
Do not import fluorine lone pairs into a nitrogen-centred count; the total around N is four.

questions.stem: A student counts the double bond in H2C=O as two separate directions and predicts four domains around carbon. Locate the counting error and give the corrected domain count.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: A direct error diagnosis once bond order is separated from the number of central directions.

qrt.X: the specific step where bond order was mistaken for number of electron-domain directions
qrt.Y: the learner can identify that carbon is bonded to two H atoms and one O atom
qrt.Z: recount distinct carbon-centred regions using one region for a multiple bond to one neighbour
qrt.W: name the counting error and give the corrected total of three
qrt.wrong_idea: A double bond automatically contributes two central electron domains because it is drawn with two lines.
qrt.replacement_rule: Bond order is not the domain count; count spatial regions/directions around the central atom.

answer.summary: The error is treating the two components/lines of the C=O double bond as two independent directions from carbon. Around carbon there are two C–H domains and one C=O domain, so the corrected electron-domain count is 3.
reasoning: Identify the counting rule: one region for each distinct bonding direction/neighbour, plus central lone-pair regions.
The C=O double bond points from carbon toward one oxygen, so it supplies one region, not two.
Add the two C–H regions: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 domains.

questions.stem: The benchmark supplies this table: BF3 has three bonding domains and no central lone pair; CH4 has four bonding domains and no central lone pair. Match each central atom to the introductory sp2 or sp3 model, and check that the number of hybrid-orbital directions agrees with the domain count.
questions.authorship_disclosure: Coordinator/AI-drafted benchmark input supplied under the owner's pilot; not an official exam/PYQ and not represented as personally authored by the owner.

difficulty.basis: Direct use of the supplied three-domain/four-domain table followed by a consistency check on hybrid-orbital set size.

qrt.X: the supplied three-domain BF3 and four-domain CH4 cases and the required sp2/sp3 mapping
qrt.Y: the introductory rule that the hybrid set has as many hybrid orbitals/directions as atomic orbitals combined
qrt.Z: map 3 → sp2 and 4 → sp3, then compare each set size with its domain count
qrt.W: state both matches and verify three versus four hybrid directions
qrt.wrong_idea: Treating the superscript as the number of hybrid orbitals, so sp2 is said to have two hybrids and sp3 three.
qrt.replacement_rule: The set size is one s plus the stated number of p orbitals: sp2 gives three hybrids and sp3 gives four.

answer.summary: BF3: three bonding domains and no central lone pair correspond to the introductory sp2 model, which provides three hybrid-orbital directions and a trigonal-planar electron-domain arrangement. CH4: four bonding domains and no central lone pair correspond to sp3, which provides four hybrid-orbital directions and a tetrahedral arrangement. In each case the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of electron-domain directions being modelled.
reasoning: Use the supplied domain counts rather than inferring from the formula alone.
Map three domains to sp2 and four domains to sp3 in the introductory hybrid model.
Check set size: one s + two p gives three sp2 hybrids; one s + three p gives four sp3 hybrids, matching the respective domain counts.
